name: Gladstone
tagline: A working port on Queensland's largest natural harbour, with island and lake escapes.
description: Gladstone is a coastal industrial city between Bundaberg and Rockhampton, built around Queensland's largest natural harbour. Auckland Point looks over the harbour, marina and ports, and Tondoon Botanic Gardens offers rainforest walks just south of the centre. Ferries from the marina reach Curtis Island and Great Barrier Reef trips, and Facing Island and Lake Awoonga sit within easy reach. Free guided industry tours run from the visitor centre on set weekdays.
whyVisit: See the working harbour from above
Take a boat to the reef and islands

goodToKnow.title: Book industry tours
goodToKnow.detail: Free alumina refinery, smelter and power station tours leave from the marina visitor centre on set weekdays. Bookings are essential.

goodToKnow.title: Pack insect repellent
goodToKnow.detail: The botanic gardens and the wetter months bring mosquitoes. Wet season runs October to March, so repellent is worth carrying.

bestTimeBlurb: {months} are the dry season, with sunnier, less humid days for the harbour and gardens.
unverified: Tour days and operators (Wikivoyage, undated; QAL Monday, Boyne smelter Friday, power station Monday) may have changed; description says only 'set weekdays'.
Mosquito claim rests on Wikivoyage's Tondoon note; wet-season link is inference.

name: Bundaberg
tagline: Rum, ginger beer and sugar-cane country, with turtle beaches and southern reef gateways.
description: Bundaberg is a sugar city on the Burnett River, about 4.5 hours north of Brisbane, and the home of Bundaberg Rum and Bundaberg Ginger Beer. Its Botanic Gardens hold the Hinkler Hall of Aviation, honouring local aviator Bert Hinkler. The Hummock gives views over the city and out to sea, while Mon Repos and Bargara sit on the beaches about 10 km away. It is also known as the southern gateway to the Great Barrier Reef, with reef trips to Lady Musgrave and Lady Elliot islands.
whyVisit: Tour the rum distillery and ginger beer brewery
Watch turtles nest at Mon Repos
Head out to the southern Great Barrier Reef

goodToKnow.title: Turtles need a ranger
goodToKnow.detail: Mon Repos turtles lay from around December and hatchlings emerge to about February, always at night. You can only watch with a ranger.

goodToKnow.title: Stay by the beach
goodToKnow.detail: The ocean beaches at Bargara and Mon Repos are about 10 km from the town centre, and Bargara has most of the beachside accommodation.

bestTimeBlurb: {months} are mild and dry. Turtle nesting and hatching runs roughly Dec–Feb.
unverified: Best months inferred from Wikipedia climate (hot wet summers, very mild dry winters); no guidebook best-time line fetched.
Turtle dates from Wikivoyage (Dec laying, ~Feb hatching); official Mon Repos season (usually Nov-Mar) not fetched.
Mon Repos Bargara and Rum Distillery are not in the sampled spot list; distillery is on Wikivoyage.

name: K'gari
tagline: The world's largest sand island, with clear freshwater lakes and rainforest on dunes.
description: K'gari, formerly Fraser Island, is a sand island about 122 km long off Queensland's southern coast, and was inscribed as a World Heritage Site in 1992. It has over 100 freshwater lakes, coloured sand cliffs and tall rainforest growing on sand dunes, and most of it is Great Sandy National Park. The main beach doubles as a highway for 4WDs, passing Eli Creek, the SS Maheno wreck and Indian Head. Dingoes live wild here, and visitors are asked to keep food secured and never feed them.
whyVisit: Drive the beach highway in a 4WD
Walk rainforest growing on sand dunes
Spot rays, turtles and dolphins from headlands

goodToKnow.title: Vehicle permit required
goodToKnow.detail: Every vehicle travelling to K'gari needs a permit on the windscreen, and campers outside commercial campgrounds need a camping permit. Get both before you go.

goodToKnow.title: 4WD and barge only
goodToKnow.detail: Vehicles cross by barge from River Heads or Inskip Point, and the sand roads need a 4WD. Allow about three days, or take a guided tour if unsure.

goodToKnow.title: Stay dingo safe
goodToKnow.detail: Feeding dingoes carries a $250 fine. Lock food away when unattended, and skip ocean swimming, where surf and sharks are a risk.

bestTimeBlurb: {months} are the dry, mild months, with humpback whales passing in Jul–Aug.
unverified: Permit prices and where to buy are not stated; permit offices on Wikivoyage are likely outdated, so none are named in the app text.
$250 dingo fine is Wikivoyage's figure; current penalty may differ.
Best months inferred from Wikivoyage climate (dry mild winters, whales Jul-Aug); Wikipedia notes crocodile sightings Dec-Mar are rare. No guidebook best-time line fetched.
Whales are seen from Platypus Bay on licensed tours from Hervey Bay; the blurb only says they pass.

name: Whitsundays
tagline: Seventy-four islands of white sand, turquoise water and reef on the Great Barrier Reef.
description: The Whitsundays are a group of 74 islands off Queensland's coast, forming part of the Great Barrier Reef, and most are national parks. Whitehaven Beach, about 4.5 km of fine white silica sand on Whitsunday Island, is the best-known image. Day trips from Airlie Beach typically combine the beach, a snorkelling stop and lunch, while resorts on islands such as Hamilton, Daydream and South Molle offer places to stay. Many other islands have only campsites.
whyVisit: Walk Whitehaven Beach's white silica sand
Snorkel coral reefs and island bays

goodToKnow.title: Book day trips early
goodToKnow.detail: Most day trips leave Airlie Beach for Whitehaven, a snorkel stop and lunch. Hamilton Island is busiest in Sep–Oct and at Christmas, so book ahead.

goodToKnow.title: Two airports
goodToKnow.detail: Hamilton Island and Proserpine both have airports, and ferries are timed to meet most flights to reach Airlie Beach and the resort islands.

goodToKnow.title: Camping on islands
goodToKnow.detail: Most islands are national parks without accommodation, but many have campsites. Bring your own water and supplies.

bestTimeBlurb: {months} are the drier months, with sunnier days for sailing, snorkelling and beach time.

name: Townsville
tagline: A sunny tropical city on a calm bay, with Magnetic Island and the Yongala wreck nearby.
description: Townsville is a laid-back coastal city of about 174,000 people in North Queensland, with an average of 320 days of sunshine a year. Castle Hill rises in the city centre with views east to Magnetic Island, and The Strand runs along the beachfront with a rockpool and cafes. Reef HQ Aquarium and the Museum of Tropical Queensland sit side by side on Flinders Street. It is the closest large centre to the SS Yongala wreck, one of Australia's top dive sites.
whyVisit: Walk Castle Hill for city views

goodToKnow.title: Humid summers
goodToKnow.detail: Summer is hot, humid and wet, with the most rain in Jan–Mar. Winter is dry and mild, so plan outdoor sightseeing for then.

goodToKnow.title: Magnetic Island ferry
goodToKnow.detail: Passenger and car ferries reach Magnetic Island in about 25 minutes, so it works as an easy day trip.

goodToKnow.title: Yongala needs experience
goodToKnow.detail: Day trips to the Yongala leave from Townsville and Magnetic Island, and operators ask for at least six logged dives.

bestTimeBlurb: {months} are dry and sunny, avoiding the humid, wet summer downpours.
unverified: Best months inferred from Wikivoyage climate chart (rain Dec-Mar, dry May-Oct); no guide best-time line fetched.
'Six logged dives' from Wikivoyage's older operator listing; check current requirements.
